newsitem.title: CUBA: Castro muses on his life, during rare public homage.
newsitem.headline: Castro muses on his life, during rare public homage.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro, who turned 70 earlier this year, said on Thursday he felt like any normal person, but also privileged to have reached this age.

Castro, who turned 70 on Aug. 13, was speaking at a ceremony in Havana to award prizes for a literary contest to honour his birthday, organised by Ecuadoran painter Osvaldo Guayasamin. The event was a rare public homage in Cuba to the life and work of the veteran communist leader.
Castro, in power for 37 years, told the gathering that he felt "like any other man, with the defects of any man."

"I never thought I would reach 70 because it seems to me a very large figure, a long time," he said. "I also don't think there is any merit in reaching this age because there are Cubans who were far better than me who did not reach 70."
"I would like to live to 80," Castro told the gathering, which included senior Communist Party leaders and government ministers.

Castro said his 50 years of "revolutionary struggle" was quite a long time, but he added, "I recall with sadness people who came before me, who fought for almost 100 years and who did not live to enjoy the independence of this nation."
He said he wondered whether he deserved such homage.

The Cuban president, in power since his rebel army overthrew former dictator Fulgencio Batista in 1959, said on the occasion of his birthday in August that while he was aware of his own mortality, the revolution he had led would not die with him.

The ceremony was to give prizes to the three winners of a literary contest on the life and works of the Cuban leader. The winners were Vietnamese Pham Tung Thien, Ecuadorian Carlos Oramas and Cuban Martha Perez Leyva.

The contest was organised by a foundation headed by Guayasamin, which presented a book with the winning and commended entries to the competition, as well as other writings on Castro. More than 2,000 people from countries around the world sent in entries to the contest.
Such an overt celebration of Castro was rare in Cuba. Although he does dominate Cuban politics, he is said to scorn the cult of the personality.
